source: A Heat Transfer Textbook, Sixth Edition, §1.2

blocks.text: 1.2 Relation of heat transfer to thermodynamics
The First Law

The subject of thermodynamics, as taught in engineering programs, makes constant reference to the heat transfer between systems. The First Law of Thermodynamics for a closed system takes the following form on a rate basis:

blocks.alt: Energy balance for a closed system. Heat transfer into the system is positive; work transfer away from the system is positive; dU/dt is positive when the system's energy increases.
blocks.explanation: Q̇ is positive toward the system, Ẇₖ is positive away from the system, and dU/dt is positive when the internal energy increases.

blocks.text: Q̇ is the heat transfer rate and Ẇₖ is the work transfer rate. They may be expressed in joules per second (J/s) or watts (W). The derivative dU/dt is the rate of change of internal thermal energy U with time t. This interaction is sketched schematically in Fig. 1.1a.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.1. The First Law of Thermodynamics for a closed system.
blocks.alt: Two diagrams of a closed system. In (a), heat enters the system, work transfer leaves it, and internal energy increases. In (b), there is no work transfer; heat enters and internal energy increases.
blocks.description: The arrows indicate the sign convention. In (a), heat entering the system and work leaving it are positive. In (b), no work is transferred.

blocks.text: The analysis of heat transfer processes can generally be done without reference to any work processes, although heat transfer might subsequently be combined with work in the analysis of real systems. If p dV work is the only work that occurs, then eqn. (1.1) is

blocks.alt: The heat transfer rate equals pressure p times the rate of volume change dV/dt plus the rate of change of internal energy dU/dt.
blocks.explanation: The energy balance when p dV work is the only work transfer.

blocks.text: This equation has two well-known special cases:

blocks.expression: Constant volume process:　Q̇ = dU/dt = m cᵥ (dT/dt)
blocks.alt: At constant volume, heat transfer rate equals the rate of change of internal energy and m c_v dT/dt.

blocks.expression: Constant pressure process:　Q̇ = dH/dt = m cₚ (dT/dt)
blocks.alt: At constant pressure, heat transfer rate equals the rate of change of enthalpy and m c_p dT/dt.

blocks.text: Here H ≡ U + pV is the enthalpy, and cᵥ and cₚ are the specific heat capacities at constant volume and constant pressure, respectively.
When the substance undergoing the process is incompressible (so that V is constant for any pressure variation), the two specific heats are equal: cᵥ = cₚ ≡ c. The proper form of eqn. (1.2a) is then

blocks.alt: For an incompressible substance, heat transfer rate equals the rate of change of internal energy and m c dT/dt.
blocks.explanation: Since solids and liquids can frequently be approximated as incompressible, this equation is used often.

blocks.text: This is as in Fig. 1.1b. Since solids and liquids can frequently be approximated as being incompressible, we shall often make use of eqn. (1.3).
If the heat transfer were reversible, then eqn. (1.2a) would become

blocks.alt: For a reversible process, heat transfer rate equals absolute temperature T times the entropy rate dS/dt, and also equals the p dV work rate plus the internal energy rate.
blocks.explanation: The subscript rev denotes a reversible process. This relation cannot be applied directly to actual irreversible heat transfer.

blocks.text: That might seem to suggest that Q̇ can be evaluated independently for inclusion in either eqn. (1.1) or (1.3). However, it cannot be evaluated using T dS, because real heat transfer processes are all irreversible and S is not defined as a function of T in an irreversible process. The reader will recall that engineering thermodynamics might better be named thermostatics, because it only describes the equilibrium states on either side of irreversible processes.
Since the rate of heat transfer cannot be predicted using T dS, how can it be determined? If U(t) were known, then (when Ẇₖ = 0) eqn. (1.3) would give Q̇, but U(t) is seldom known a priori.

The answer is that a new set of physical principles must be introduced to predict Q̇. The principles are transport laws, which are not a part of the subject of thermodynamics. They include Fourier's law, Newton's law of cooling, and the Stefan-Boltzmann law. We introduce these laws later in the chapter. The important thing to remember is that a description of heat transfer requires that additional principles be combined with the First Law of Thermodynamics.
Reversible heat transfer as the temperature gradient vanishes

Consider a wall connecting two thermal reservoirs as shown in Fig. 1.2. As long as T₁ > T₂, heat will flow spontaneously and irreversibly from 1 to 2. In accordance with our understanding of the Second Law of Thermodynamics, we expect the entropy of the universe to increase as a consequence of this process. If T₂ approaches T₁, the process will approach being quasistatic and reversible. But the rate of heat transfer will also approach zero if there is no temperature difference to drive it. Thus all real heat transfer processes generate entropy.

blocks.caption: Figure 1.2. Irreversible heat flow between two thermal reservoirs through an intervening wall.
blocks.alt: Thermal reservoir 1 at temperature T1 and a cooler reservoir 2 at T2 are separated by a wall. In steady conduction, the temperature profile in the wall decreases from T1 to T2 along distance x.
blocks.description: A temperature difference T₁ − T₂ drives heat from the hotter reservoir 1 to the cooler reservoir 2. The plotted wall temperature profile is an example of steady state.

blocks.text: Now we come to a dilemma: If the irreversible process occurs at steady state, the properties of the wall do not vary with time. We know that the entropy of the wall depends on its state and must therefore be constant. How, then, does the entropy of the universe increase? We turn to this question next.
Entropy production

The entropy increase of the universe as the result of a process is the sum of the entropy changes of all elements that are involved in that process. The rate of entropy production of the universe, Ṡ_Un, resulting from the preceding heat transfer process through a wall is

blocks.alt: The universe's entropy production rate is the sum of the entropy rates of reservoir 1, the wall, and reservoir 2. At steady state Ṡ_wall=0.
blocks.explanation: res denotes a reservoir, wall denotes the wall, and Un denotes the universe. At steady state the wall's entropy is constant, so Ṡ_wall = 0.

blocks.text: The dots denote time derivatives (e.g., ẋ ≡ dx/dt). Since the reservoir temperatures are constant,

blocks.alt: For a reservoir at constant temperature, its entropy rate equals the heat transfer rate into it divided by its temperature.
blocks.explanation: The sign of Q̇_res is positive into the reservoir.

blocks.text: Now Q̇_res,1 is negative and equal in magnitude to Q̇_res,2, so eqn. (1.5) becomes

blocks.alt: The universe's entropy production rate equals the magnitude of heat leaving reservoir 1 times 1/T2 minus 1/T1. It is positive when T1 is greater than T2.
blocks.explanation: The term in parentheses is positive when T₁ > T₂, so Ṡ_Un > 0. This agrees with Clausius's statement of the Second Law of Thermodynamics.

blocks.text: Notice an odd fact here: The rate of heat transfer, Q̇, and hence Ṡ_Un, is determined by the wall's resistance to heat flow. Although the wall is the agent that causes the entropy of the universe to increase, its own entropy does not change. Only the entropies of the reservoirs change.
T = absolute temperature, S = entropy, V = volume, p = pressure, and rev denotes a reversible process.
